\hlchaptermodality{517}

\section[el testigo]{el testigo — the witness}

\label{lesson:ES-C517-testigo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to refute, then the Spanish for the version.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el testigo}
\textbf{el testigo} — \textquotedblleft{}the witness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Un testigo llamó a la policía.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A witness called the police.}
\end{quote}

The same form for a woman: \emph{la testigo}. \emph{Ser testigo de algo} is to witness it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{testigo} comes from old Spanish \emph{testiguar} 'to bear witness' (EtymDB), which goes back to Latin \emph{testificārī}, built on \emph{testis} 'a witness'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el testigo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el testigo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el testigo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to refute, then the Spanish for the version, then say \emph{el testigo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el testigo mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The witness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[presenciar]{presenciar — to witness, to be present at}

\label{lesson:ES-C517-presenciar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the version, then the Spanish for the witness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: presenciar}
\textbf{presenciar} — \textquotedblleft{}to witness, to be present at\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Presencié el accidente desde la ventana.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I witnessed the accident from the window.}
\end{quote}

It takes a direct object: \emph{presenciar un partido} — to watch a match in person.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{presenciar} is built on \emph{presencia} 'presence', which comes from Latin \emph{praesentia} 'a being at hand' (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{praesēns} 'present'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{presenciar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{presenciar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the version, then the Spanish for the witness, then say \emph{presenciar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[observar]{observar — to observe, to watch}

\label{lesson:ES-C517-observar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the witness, then the Spanish for to witness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: observar}
\textbf{observar} — \textquotedblleft{}to observe, to watch\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La vecina lo observaba todo desde la ventana.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The neighbour was watching everything from the window.}
\end{quote}

It also means to remark: \emph{Observó que era tarde.}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{observar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{observāre} 'to watch, to heed' (EtymDB), built on \emph{ob-} and \emph{servāre} 'to keep, to guard'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{observar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{observar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{observar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the witness, then the Spanish for to witness, then say \emph{observar} again
\end{itemize}

\section[percatarse]{percatarse — to notice, to realise}

\label{lesson:ES-C517-percatarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to witness, then the Spanish for to observe.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: percatarse}
\textbf{percatarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to notice, to realise\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No me percaté de nada aquella noche.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I didn't notice anything that night.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Percatarse de algo} — to notice something. A little formal; in speech, \emph{darse cuenta}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{percatarse} is built on old Spanish \emph{catar} 'to see, to examine' with \emph{per-}. \emph{Catar} is usually traced to Latin \emph{captāre} 'to try to catch', from \emph{capere} 'to take'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el detalle]{el detalle — the detail}

\label{lesson:ES-C517-detalle}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to observe, then the Spanish for to notice.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el detalle}
\textbf{el detalle} — \textquotedblleft{}the detail\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Recuerdo cada detalle de aquel día.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I remember every detail of that day.}
\end{quote}

\emph{¡Qué detalle!} — how thoughtful! — said about a small kind gesture.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{detalle} was borrowed from French \emph{détail}, which is usually traced to \emph{tailler} 'to cut', from Late Latin \emph{taliāre}. A detail is a small piece cut off from the whole.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
